The supplied proof rests on three independent linear-algebra facts. Each becomes a child, and no child depends on another:
(1) oriented_frame (proof step 1): there is an orthonormal frame σ of ν^⊥ with det[ν, σ] = −1.
(2) covector_det_rep (steps 2–4): every n-covector on ℝ^{n+1} equals a ↦ det[φ_β, a]. This is the classical Hodge-dual / cofactor identity (cf. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hodge_star_operator; Laplace-expansion form in arXiv:1112.1346) and the main technical obligation.
(3) det_normal_decomp (the determinant argument of step 5): det[w, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ] whenever span σ = (span{ν})^⊥.

- Linearity gives ⟨φ_β, ν⟩ = Σ_j (−1)^j b_j ⟨e_j, ν⟩, which is the frozen conclusion.

subproblems.title: A negatively oriented orthonormal frame σ of ν^⊥: det[ν, σ] = −1
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and ν ∈ ℝ^{n+1} with |ν| = 1. For x ∈ ℝ^{n+1} and a family a = (a_0, …, a_{n−1}) in ℝ^{n+1}, let [x, a] be the (n+1)×(n+1) real matrix whose column 0 is x and whose column l+1 is a_l (its entry in row r, column c is the r-th coordinate of the c-th column vector). Then there is an orthonormal family σ = (σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}) in ℝ^{n+1} with span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}} = (span{ν})^⊥ and det[ν, σ] = −1.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (ν : Euclid (n + 1)), 1 ≤ n → ‖ν‖ = 1 → ∃ σ : Fin n → Euclid (n + 1), Orthonormal ℝ σ ∧ Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range σ) = (Submodule.span ℝ {ν})ᗮ ∧ Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun r c : Fin (n + 1) => (Fin.cons ν σ : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r) = -1
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 (Oriented frame) of the parent proof, with the sign normalization written uniformly.

Notation. ⟨·,·⟩ is the standard inner product of ℝ^{n+1} and x_r is the r-th coordinate of x ∈ ℝ^{n+1}. For x ∈ ℝ^{n+1} and a = (a_0, …, a_{n−1}), [x, a] is the matrix with entries [x, a]_{r,c} = (c-th vector of (x, a_0, …, a_{n−1}))_r; in Lean it is Matrix.of fun r c => (Fin.cons x a : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r, so column 0 holds x and column l+1 (= Fin.succ l) holds a_l. Indices of σ and τ range over Fin n = {0, …, n−1}.

1. (Dimension.) Since |ν| = 1, ν ≠ 0, so span{ν} is 1-dimensional and Q := (span{ν})^⊥ has dimension (n+1) − 1 = n, because dim V + dim V^⊥ = dim ℝ^{n+1} = n+1 for every subspace V (Mathlib: Submodule.finrank_orthogonal_span_singleton, with finrank ℝ (Euclid (n+1)) = n+1 from finrank_euclideanSpace_fin).
2. (Orthonormal basis of Q.) Choose an orthonormal basis (q_0, …, q_{n−1}) of Q indexed by Fin n (for instance stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ Q reindexed along finCongr of the equality finrank Q = n from step 1), and let τ_k ∈ ℝ^{n+1} be q_k regarded as a vector of ℝ^{n+1}. The inner product of Q is the restriction of that of ℝ^{n+1}, so τ = (τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) is orthonormal in ℝ^{n+1} (Orthonormal.comp_linearIsometry with the inclusion Q.subtypeₗᵢ). The q_k span Q, so the τ_k span the image of Q under the inclusion, which is Q itself: span{τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}} = Q (Submodule.span_image, Submodule.map_top, Submodule.range_subtype).
3. (τ_k ⊥ ν.) Each τ_k lies in Q = (span{ν})^⊥, hence ⟨ν, τ_k⟩ = 0 (Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right).
4. (u := (ν, τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) is an orthonormal basis of ℝ^{n+1}.) Put u_0 := ν and u_{l+1} := τ_l, i.e. u = Fin.cons ν τ. Then ⟨u_0, u_0⟩ = |ν|² = 1; ⟨u_0, u_{l+1}⟩ = ⟨u_{l+1}, u_0⟩ = ⟨ν, τ_l⟩ = 0 by step 3 and symmetry; and ⟨u_{l+1}, u_{m+1}⟩ = ⟨τ_l, τ_m⟩ = δ_{lm} by step 2. So u is an orthonormal family of n+1 vectors (orthonormal_iff_ite, checked by cases on whether each index is 0 or a successor). It is linearly independent, and since its cardinality n+1 equals dim ℝ^{n+1}, it spans ℝ^{n+1} (LinearIndependent.span_eq_top_of_card_eq_finrank'); hence u is an orthonormal basis of ℝ^{n+1} (OrthonormalBasis.mk).
5. (d := det[ν, τ] satisfies d·d = 1.) Let W := [ν, τ], so W_{r,c} = (u_c)_r. For all c, c' we have (WᵀW)_{c,c'} = Σ_r (u_c)_r (u_{c'})_r = ⟨u_c, u_{c'}⟩ = δ_{cc'}, so WᵀW = I and d² = det(Wᵀ)·det(W) = det(WᵀW) = 1. (Equivalently: det W is the determinant of the orthonormal basis u with respect to the standard orthonormal basis EuclideanSpace.basisFun, by Module.Basis.det_apply, and that determinant is 1 or −1 by OrthonormalBasis.det_to_matrix_orthonormalBasis_real.) Hence d ∈ {1, −1} and d·d = 1.
6. (Sign normalization.) Since n ≥ 1, the index 0 ∈ Fin n exists. Define σ_0 := (−d)·τ_0 and σ_l := τ_l for l ≠ 0, i.e. σ := Function.update τ 0 ((−d)•τ_0). (If d = 1 this replaces τ_0 by −τ_0; if d = −1 it leaves τ unchanged — exactly the case distinction of the parent proof.)
7. (σ is orthonormal.) ⟨σ_0, σ_0⟩ = (−d)²⟨τ_0, τ_0⟩ = d·d = 1. For l ≠ 0: ⟨σ_0, σ_l⟩ = (−d)⟨τ_0, τ_l⟩ = 0 and ⟨σ_l, σ_0⟩ = (−d)⟨τ_l, τ_0⟩ = 0. For l, m ≠ 0: ⟨σ_l, σ_m⟩ = ⟨τ_l, τ_m⟩ = δ_{lm}. Hence ⟨σ_l, σ_m⟩ = δ_{lm} for all l, m, i.e. σ is orthonormal (orthonormal_iff_ite).
8. (span σ = (span{ν})^⊥.) Each σ_l is a scalar multiple of τ_l, so every σ_l lies in span{τ} and span{σ} ⊆ span{τ}. Conversely, τ_0 = (−d)·σ_0 because (−d)·(−d) = d·d = 1, and τ_l = σ_l for l ≠ 0, so every τ_l lies in span{σ} and span{τ} ⊆ span{σ}. Therefore span{σ} = span{τ} = Q = (span{ν})^⊥ by step 2.
9. (det[ν, σ] = −1.) The matrices [ν, σ] and W coincide except in column 1 = Fin.succ 0, which holds σ_0 = (−d)·τ_0 in [ν, σ] and τ_0 in W; indeed Fin.cons ν (Function.update τ 0 y) = Function.update (Fin.cons ν τ) (Fin.succ 0) y (Fin.cons_update). The determinant is linear in each column (Matrix.det_updateCol_smul; equivalently AlternatingMap.map_update_smul for the standard-basis determinant), so det[ν, σ] = (−d)·det W = −(d·d) = −1.
10. By steps 7, 8 and 9, σ is an orthonormal family in ℝ^{n+1} with span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}} = (span{ν})^⊥ and det[ν, σ] = −1. ∎
proof_key_steps: Q = (span{ν})^⊥ has dimension n; an orthonormal basis τ of Q (stdOrthonormalBasis reindexed to Fin n) is orthonormal in ℝ^{n+1}, spans Q, and satisfies ⟨ν, τ_k⟩ = 0.
(ν, τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) is an orthonormal basis of ℝ^{n+1}, so d := det[ν, τ] is the determinant of an orthogonal matrix and d·d = 1.
Replace τ_0 by (−d)·τ_0 (possible as n ≥ 1): orthonormality and the span are preserved, and linearity of det in column 1 gives det[ν, σ] = −d·d = −1.

subproblems.title: Every n-covector on ℝ^{n+1} is the determinant with first column φ_β
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 0 and let β be an n-covector on ℝ^{n+1} (a continuous alternating n-linear form). Let e_0, …, e_n be the standard basis of ℝ^{n+1}, j.succAbove the increasing enumeration of {0, …, n} ∖ {j}, b_j := β(e_{j.succAbove 0}, …, e_{j.succAbove(n−1)}) for j ∈ {0, …, n}, and φ_β := Σ_{j=0}^{n} (−1)^j b_j e_j. For x ∈ ℝ^{n+1} and a = (a_0, …, a_{n−1}) in ℝ^{n+1}, let [x, a] be the (n+1)×(n+1) real matrix whose column 0 is x and whose column l+1 is a_l (its entry in row r, column c is the r-th coordinate of the c-th column vector). Then β(a_0, …, a_{n−1}) = det[φ_β, a] for every a = (a_0, …, a_{n−1}) ∈ (ℝ^{n+1})^n.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (β : Covector (Euclid (n + 1)) n) (a : Fin n → Euclid (n + 1)), β a = Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun r c : Fin (n + 1) => (Fin.cons (∑ j : Fin (n + 1), ((-1 : ℝ) ^ (j : ℕ) * β (fun k => EuclideanSpace.single (j.succAbove k) (1 : ℝ))) • EuclideanSpace.single j (1 : ℝ)) a : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 2–4 of the parent proof (multilinear expansion of β, Laplace expansion along the first column, and their combination), organized as a comparison of two alternating maps on basis tuples.

Notation. x_r is the r-th coordinate of x ∈ ℝ^{n+1}, so (e_i)_r = 1 if r = i and 0 otherwise. For a map s : Fin n → Fin (n+1), e_s := (e_{s(0)}, …, e_{s(n−1)}); in particular e_{j.succAbove} := (e_{j.succAbove 0}, …, e_{j.succAbove(n−1)}), so b_j = β(e_{j.succAbove}). Write φ := φ_β; its j-th coordinate is φ_j = (−1)^j b_j. In Lean, e_j = EuclideanSpace.single j 1 = EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin (n+1)) ℝ j (EuclideanSpace.basisFun_apply) and [x, a] = Matrix.of fun r c => (Fin.cons x a : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r; for v : Fin (n+1) → ℝ^{n+1}, det(Matrix.of fun r c => v c r) = det_std(v), the determinant with respect to the standard basis (Module.Basis.det_apply).

1. (Laplace expansion; parent step 3.) For x ∈ ℝ^{n+1} and a ∈ (ℝ^{n+1})^n, expansion along column 0 (Matrix.det_succ_column_zero) gives
   det[x, a] = Σ_{i=0}^{n} (−1)^i x_i det M_i(a),  where M_i(a)_{k,l} := (a_l)_{i.succAbove k} for k, l ∈ Fin n,
   because the entry of [x, a] in row i and column 0 is x_i, and deleting row i and column 0 leaves the entries [x, a]_{i.succAbove k, l+1} = (a_l)_{i.succAbove k}.
2. (Both sides are alternating n-linear in a.) F(a) := β(a) is alternating and n-linear by hypothesis. G(a) := det[φ, a] is n-linear in a, because a_l occupies only column l+1 and the determinant is linear in each column; it is alternating, because a_l = a_{l'} with l ≠ l' produces two equal columns and hence determinant 0. (In Lean, G = (det_std).curryLeft φ by AlternatingMap.curryLeft_apply_apply.)
3. (Reduction to injective basis tuples; parent step 2.) Expanding a_l = Σ_r (a_l)_r e_r in every argument and using multilinearity, every n-linear map H satisfies H(a) = Σ_{s : Fin n → Fin (n+1)} (Π_l (a_l)_{s(l)}) H(e_s). Hence F = G as soon as F(e_s) = G(e_s) for every s : Fin n → Fin (n+1). If s is not injective, e_s has two equal entries, so F(e_s) = 0 = G(e_s) because F and G are alternating. Therefore it suffices to prove F(e_s) = G(e_s) for every injective s. (This reduction is Module.Basis.ext_alternating for the standard basis.)
4. (An injective tuple is a permuted sorted tuple; parent step 2.) Let s : Fin n → Fin (n+1) be injective. Some j ∈ Fin (n+1) is not a value of s: otherwise s would map the n-element set Fin n onto the (n+1)-element set Fin (n+1), which is impossible (Fintype.card_le_of_surjective). For each l we have s(l) ≠ j, so s(l) = j.succAbove(ρ(l)) for some ρ(l) ∈ Fin n (Fin.exists_succAbove_eq). If ρ(l) = ρ(l'), then s(l) = s(l') and hence l = l'; so ρ is an injective self-map of the finite set Fin n and therefore a permutation of Fin n (Finite.injective_iff_bijective, Equiv.ofBijective). Consequently e_s = e_{j.succAbove} ∘ ρ.
5. (Sign bookkeeping.) For every alternating map H and permutation ρ, H(v ∘ ρ) = sign(ρ)·H(v) (AlternatingMap.map_perm). Hence F(e_s) = sign(ρ)·F(e_{j.succAbove}) and G(e_s) = sign(ρ)·G(e_{j.succAbove}). Since F(e_{j.succAbove}) = b_j by definition, it remains to show G(e_{j.succAbove}) = det[φ, e_{j.succAbove}] = b_j for every j ∈ Fin (n+1).
6. (The sorted tuple; parent steps 3–4.) Fix j and put a := e_{j.succAbove}. By step 1, det[φ, a] = Σ_i (−1)^i φ_i det M_i(a), where M_i(a)_{k,l} = (e_{j.succAbove l})_{i.succAbove k} equals 1 if i.succAbove k = j.succAbove l and 0 otherwise.
   (a) i = j: j.succAbove is injective, so M_j(a)_{k,l} = 1 exactly when k = l; M_j(a) is the identity matrix and det M_j(a) = 1.
   (b) i ≠ j: then i = j.succAbove(l₀) for some l₀ ∈ Fin n (Fin.exists_succAbove_eq). The entries of column l₀ of M_i(a) are (e_i)_{i.succAbove k}, and these are all 0 because i.succAbove k ≠ i for every k (Fin.succAbove_ne). A matrix with a zero column has determinant 0, so det M_i(a) = 0.
   Therefore det[φ, a] = (−1)^j φ_j = (−1)^j (−1)^j b_j = ((−1)^2)^j b_j = b_j.
   (Equivalent computation using linearity in column 0 instead of minors: det[φ, a] = Σ_i (−1)^i b_i det[e_i, a]. For i ≠ j, with l₀ as in (b), columns 0 and l₀+1 of [e_i, a] are both e_i, so det[e_i, a] = 0 (AlternatingMap.map_eq_zero_of_eq). For i = j, the tuple (e_j, e_{j.succAbove 0}, …, e_{j.succAbove(n−1)}) is the standard basis composed with the permutation π := (Fin.cycleRange j)^{−1}, because π(0) = j and π(l+1) = j.succAbove l (Fin.cycleRange_symm_zero, Fin.cycleRange_symm_succ); hence det[e_j, a] = sign(π)·det_std(e_0, …, e_n) = sign(Fin.cycleRange j) = (−1)^j (AlternatingMap.map_perm, Module.Basis.det_self, Equiv.Perm.sign_symm, Fin.sign_cycleRange). Either way det[φ, a] = (−1)^j(−1)^j b_j = b_j.)
7. By steps 4–6, F(e_s) = G(e_s) for every injective s : Fin n → Fin (n+1); by step 3, F = G, i.e. β(a) = det[φ_β, a] for every a ∈ (ℝ^{n+1})^n. (For n = 0 the argument applies verbatim: the only s is the empty map, j = 0, ρ is the empty permutation, and det[φ] = φ_0 = b_0 = β of the empty tuple.) ∎
proof_key_steps: Laplace expansion along column 0: det[x, a] = Σ_i (−1)^i x_i det M_i(a) with M_i(a)_{k,l} = (a_l)_{i.succAbove k}; both β and a ↦ det[φ_β, a] are alternating n-linear in a.

By multilinear expansion (Module.Basis.ext_alternating) it suffices to compare them on injective standard-basis tuples e_s; an injective s equals j.succAbove ∘ ρ for a missed index j and a permutation ρ, and both sides scale by sign ρ.
At the sorted tuple e_{j.succAbove} only the i = j Laplace term survives, so det[φ_β, e_{j.succAbove}] = (−1)^j(−1)^j b_j = b_j = β(e_{j.succAbove}).

subproblems.title: det[w, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ] when span σ = (span{ν})^⊥
subproblems.statement: Let n ≥ 0, let ν, w ∈ ℝ^{n+1} with |ν| = 1, and let σ = (σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}) be a family in ℝ^{n+1} with span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}} = (span{ν})^⊥. For x ∈ ℝ^{n+1} let [x, σ] be the (n+1)×(n+1) real matrix whose column 0 is x and whose column l+1 is σ_l (its entry in row r, column c is the r-th coordinate of the c-th column vector). Then det[w, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (ν w : Euclid (n + 1)) (σ : Fin n → Euclid (n + 1)), ‖ν‖ = 1 → Submodule.span ℝ (Set.range σ) = (Submodule.span ℝ {ν})ᗮ → Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun r c : Fin (n + 1) => (Fin.cons w σ : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r) = inner ℝ w ν * Matrix.det (Matrix.of fun r c : Fin (n + 1) => (Fin.cons ν σ : Fin (n + 1) → Euclid (n + 1)) c r)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: the determinant argument of step 5 of the parent proof ('the determinant is linear in its first column and vanishes when two columns are equal, so det[φ, σ] = ⟨φ, ν⟩·det[ν, σ]'), stated for an arbitrary first column w and for any family σ spanning ν^⊥ (orthonormality of σ is not used).

Notation. ⟨·,·⟩ is the standard (real, symmetric) inner product of ℝ^{n+1}, and D(x) := det[x, σ] for x ∈ ℝ^{n+1}. In Lean, det(Matrix.of fun r c => v c r) = det_std(v), the determinant with respect to the standard basis EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Module.Basis.det_apply), and D(x) = det_std(Fin.cons x σ) = (det_std.curryLeft x)(σ) (AlternatingMap.curryLeft_apply_apply).

1. (D is linear.) Column 0 of [x, σ] is the only column depending on x, and the determinant is linear in each column; hence D(x + y) = D(x) + D(y) and D(t·x) = t·D(x) for x, y ∈ ℝ^{n+1}, t ∈ ℝ. (Explicitly, Laplace expansion along column 0 gives D(x) = Σ_i (−1)^i x_i det N_i with minors N_i not depending on x; in Lean, x ↦ det_std.curryLeft x is a linear map, so map_add and map_smul apply.)
2. (D vanishes on span σ.) Let q ∈ span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}}. The family (q, σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}) = Fin.cons q σ is not linearly independent, since Fin.cons q σ is linearly independent only if q ∉ span(range σ) (linearIndependent_finCons). The determinant of a matrix whose columns are linearly dependent is 0 (AlternatingMap.map_linearDependent applied to det_std). Hence D(q) = 0. (Alternatively: write q = Σ_k c_k σ_k; by step 1, D(q) = Σ_k c_k D(σ_k), and each D(σ_k) = 0 because [σ_k, σ] has equal columns 0 and k+1.)
3. (Normal decomposition.) Put q := w − ⟨w, ν⟩ν. Using ⟨ν, ν⟩ = |ν|² = 1 and the symmetry of the real inner product, ⟨ν, q⟩ = ⟨ν, w⟩ − ⟨w, ν⟩⟨ν, ν⟩ = ⟨w, ν⟩ − ⟨w, ν⟩ = 0. Hence q ∈ (span{ν})^⊥ (Submodule.mem_orthogonal_singleton_iff_inner_right), and by the hypothesis span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}} = (span{ν})^⊥ we get q ∈ span{σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}}.
4. (Conclusion.) Since w = ⟨w, ν⟩ν + q, steps 1–3 give D(w) = ⟨w, ν⟩·D(ν) + D(q) = ⟨w, ν⟩·D(ν), that is, det[w, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ]. ∎
proof_key_steps: x ↦ det[x, σ] is linear, since only column 0 depends on x.
det[q, σ] = 0 for every q ∈ span σ, because the columns (q, σ_0, …, σ_{n−1}) are linearly dependent.
q := w − ⟨w, ν⟩ν lies in ν^⊥ = span σ, so det[w, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ] + det[q, σ] = ⟨w, ν⟩·det[ν, σ].
